title: A distorted duo
caption: The interacting galaxy IC 1727, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: IC 1727, UGC 1249 · constellation Triangulum · about 23 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The galaxy IC 1727 looks twisted and lopsided in this Hubble image, and its bright nucleus has been dragged off-centre. The cause is its near neighbour NGC 672, just out of frame, with which it is interacting.

Gravity pulls galaxies together into groups and clusters, and sometimes brings pairs close enough to tug on each other. The results can be extreme. Interacting galaxies are often badly distorted, torn apart, or driven to collide and merge into a single mass of gas, dust and stars.

Such encounters often trigger starbursts, flurries of intense star formation, and new star clusters, likely because gravity churns and compacts the gas and dust. Astronomers found that both IC 1727 and NGC 672 had simultaneous bursts of star formation, roughly 20 to 30 million years ago, and again around 450 to 750 million years ago. The likeliest explanation is that the pair swing close to each other every so often, stirring up gas and dust each time they pass.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.41 x 2.38 arcminutes) and distance (23 million light years), the frame spans roughly 16,000 × 16,000 light-years. Its light set out about 23 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This image combines Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, with ultraviolet, visible, H-alpha and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and the galaxy is far too faint to see this way without a telescope.
